newsitem.title: USA: American, BA cargo customers to gain from alliance.
newsitem.headline: American, BA cargo customers to gain from alliance.

text.p: Cargo customers, particularly freight forwarders, have everything to gain and nothing to fear from the proposed American Airlines/British Airways alliance, David Brooks, president of AA Cargo, told Reuters.

The cargo part of the alliance will create a global network, with one-stop shopping for bookings and global pricing for interline moves over the two carriers, he said in an interview here at the International Air Transport Association (IATA) Cargo Week 97.
The two carriers are also working on linking their cargo reservations computers.

By coordinating schedules, standardizing processes and working out of each other's major terminals, the two airlines should be able to move interline freight faster through their shared system, Brooks added.

And by identifying efficiencies, the joint system should be more cost effective, and as an additional assurance, there will still be a great deal of competition from other airlines for the traffic they carry, he said.
However Brooks acknowledged the airlines are fighting a perception by some freight forwarders that this combined entity will face huge operational problems.

"That's why before we roll this out from the cargo perspective, we want to be sure we have all those issues resolved," said Brooks. Teams from both carriers are spending a great deal of time standardizing policies and processes as well as building the computer interfaces needed to create a single system.
The airlines are using cargo customer focus groups to identify and help overcome customers' concerns about the alliance, he said.

"It is the single cargo network that will be the biggest benefit to BA and AA as well as to shippers because we'll be able to interline, in effect, around the world with two carriers as opposed to five or six," Brooks said.
"This alliance will automate this whole process and allow a shipper or a forwarder to use our combined network as if they were talking to just one carrier," he added.
Brooks succeeded Bill Boesch as AA Cargo president in September last year.
It could be several more months before the controversial alliance gets all the regulatory approvals needed, including U.S. anti-trust immunity to set joint rates.
That rate-setting ability, and the sheer size of the network, will set it apart from AA cargo alliances with Japan Air Lines and Alitalia
Brooks said there does not appear to be a major corporate culture gap between the BA and AA cargo divisions.
"What is different is how we do some of the standard routine things," he said.

"Pricing (decisions) at American Airlines Cargo is very centralized, whereas pricing at BA World Cargo is very decentralized," he said, whilst American's processes, including booking procedures, are more automated than BA's.

"What we have to work out is that we can't operate differently and still work together. We are coming up with a hybrid way of pricing, for example, that works well for both of us and creates the most benefits for the alliance," Brooks added.
